title: Bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2)
hookLine: and so you shall fulfill the law of Christ

lines: WHAT TO DO WITH EACH OTHER'S WEIGHT.
cards: Somebody in the congregation gets caught doing something wrong, and by Sunday everyone knows. You can feel the room choose sides. Paul knew that room.
Near the end of Galatians he writes: if someone is overtaken in a fault, you who are spiritual should set him right in a spirit of gentleness, and keep an eye on yourself, in case you're tempted too.
Then, in one short verse, he tells the whole church what to do with each other's weight.

teach.h: THE LAW OF CHRIST: CARRY EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Here it is: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." The law of Christ. That's a striking phrase in this letter.
Paul has spent five chapters arguing that Gentile believers don't need to take on the law of Moses. Now he names a law they do have to keep, and it's this one: carry each other.

Christians connect it to Jesus's command at the Last Supper, to love one another as he has loved them. Then, three verses later, Paul seems to contradict himself: "For every one shall bear his own burden." Which is it?
Carry each other's, or carry your own? Many readers find that the Greek helps.
In the first verse the word is baros, a heavy, crushing weight, the kind no one should carry alone.
In the second it's phortion, a pack, like the kit a soldier is expected to carry himself. So: share the crushing weights, and carry your own daily pack.
Don't dump your pack on others, and don't leave anyone alone under a boulder.

teach.h: SIMON OF CYRENE: THE FIFTH STATION.
teach.b: Catholics see this verse acted out at the fifth station of the cross, where Simon of Cyrene is made to help Jesus carry the cross. He didn't volunteer; the soldiers pressed him into it.
Yet the Church remembers him for it, and many Catholics pray before that station every Lent.
The works of mercy put the verse into daily practice too: comfort the sorrowful, visit the sick, bear wrongs patiently. Notice that Paul doesn't say to fix each other's burdens. Often you can't.
You can only take a corner of the weight.

how: Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross, especially in Lent, including the fifth station, where Simon of Cyrene helps Jesus carry the cross; the works of mercy put bearing burdens into practice.

games.q: someone in your church has been caught in a fault, and everyone is talking. what does Paul tell you to do?
o: keep away, so it doesn't spread.
set him right gently, and watch yourself.
games.why: set him right in a spirit of gentleness, watching yourself, and "bear ye one another's burdens."

practice: Think of someone carrying something too heavy right now: an illness, a debt, a child in trouble, grief.

Don't try to solve it; just ask what one corner you could lift, a meal, a ride, an hour of sitting with them, a call where you mostly listen. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, hold them in mind with that one thing.

wordCard.voice: Baros. The crushing weight Paul says we should share for each other, not the daily pack everyone carries alone. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a heavy weight (Galatians 6:2). contrasted with phortion, a pack, in 6:5.
